metadata.title: How to improve the design of experimental studies in computing education: Evidence from the international assessments

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICILS 2013 and ICILS 2018 microdata with a complex sampling design (stratification of schools and randomization within schools for teachers and students). The authors estimate multilevel variance components (ICC, R2 at level 1/2) and compute minimum detectable effect sizes (MDES) using plausible values for the dependent constructs (CIL and CT). They report that the WeMix package was used in R, which allows sampling weights at each level separately, but the manuscript does not explicitly name the weight variables or confirm whether weights were applied in the final analyses. Because the paper focuses on power-analysis quantities derived from multilevel models rather than predictive ML performance, the weighting strategy is primarily relevant for producing accurate variance-component estimates; however, the exact weight variable(s) and whether replicate-weight variance estimation was used are not specified.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic data are drawn from ICILS 2013 and ICILS 2018 cycles for students in the 8th year of schooling (at least 13.5 years old). The 2013 cycle contributes only CIL outcomes, while the 2018 cycle contributes both CIL and CT outcomes; CT is missing for five countries in 2018 (CHL, ITA, KAZ, RMO, URY), so CT analyses exclude those countries. For model estimation (Null, Model 1, Model 2, Model 3), the manuscript notes that sample sizes for running the models could be lower than the country N due to listwise deletion of cases with missing data. Teacher covariates are incorporated at the school level by aggregating teacher measures within schools because teacher–student linkage is not available under the sampling procedures.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2013 Grade 8 Computer and information literacy (CIL)
main_findings.target_variable: CIL intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) and explained variance (R2) for CRT design
main_findings.performance_metrics: Country-specific ICC differences: 0.44 (2013). Model comparisons: Model 2 level-1 R2 nearly negligible across countries; Model 1 and Model 3 similar at level 1; all three models explain more variance at level 2 than level 1 in most countries. MDES examples (Model 1, N=20, J=10): NLD 1.7 vs SVN 0.8.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2013 Grade 8 Computer and information literacy (CIL) the study leveraged gender, interest in ICT, socioeconomic status, ICT self-efficacy, and ICT resources (via multilevel null/partial/full models) to estimate ICCs and explained variance for cluster randomized trial (CRT) design, finding that ICCs were country-specific and that adding both student-level and school/teacher-level covariates (Model 3) reduced MDES relative to models with fewer covariates. This indicates that CRTs in CIL should be powered using baseline, country-specific ICC/R2 estimates and that incorporating both student and school/teacher context variables can improve the precision of detectable effects, though the results are design/power estimates rather than causal intervention effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2018 Grade 8 Computer and information literacy (CIL)
main_findings.target_variable: CIL intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) and explained variance (R2) for CRT design
main_findings.performance_metrics: Country-specific ICC differences: 0.46 (2018). ICC range examples: DEU highest ICC (0.58) and KOR lowest ICC (0.14). Model comparisons: Model 2 level-1 R2 nearly negligible across countries; Model 1 and Model 3 similar at level 1; all three models explain large variance at level 2. MDES: Model 3 associated with smaller MDES than Models 1–2 when J≥20.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2018 Grade 8 Computer and information literacy (CIL) the study leveraged gender, interest in ICT, ICT self-efficacy, computer experience, and school/teacher ICT context variables (in multilevel null/partial/full models) to estimate ICCs and explained variance for CRT design, finding that ICCs were country-specific (e.g., DEU 0.58 vs KOR 0.14) and that Model 3 (both levels of covariates) produced smaller MDES than Models 1–2 under conditions with more schools. This indicates that planning CRTs for CIL should prioritize baseline measurement of between-school clustering and that including both student and school/teacher covariates can improve statistical efficiency, while causality of covariates on CIL is not established because the analysis is for power/design parameters.

main_findings.target_variable: CT intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) and explained variance (R2) for CRT design
main_findings.performance_metrics: ICC difference (2018): 0.38 across countries. ICC range examples: CT ICCs ranged from 0.11 to 0.49. Model comparisons: Model 1 and Model 3 explained more variance at level 1 than Model 2; all three models explained significant variance at level 2. MDES: Model 2 had slightly higher MDES than Model 1 across countries; Model 3 yielded smaller MDES only when J≥20.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2018 Grade 8 Computational thinking (CT) the study leveraged gender, ICT self-efficacy, computer experience, ICT use in classroom activities, and ICT resources at school (within two-level multilevel models) to estimate ICCs and explained variance for CRT design, finding that CT clustering varied by country (ICC range 0.11–0.49) and that adding both student and school/teacher covariates (Model 3) reduced MDES relative to models with fewer covariates when the number of schools was sufficiently large. This indicates that CT intervention trials should be designed with country-specific clustering expectations and that collecting baseline student and school/teacher ICT context can improve the precision of detectable effects, while the study does not evaluate intervention impact directly.

data.outcome_summary: This paper uses ICILS 2013 and ICILS 2018 Grade 8 data to improve the design of cluster randomized trials (CRTs) for computer and information literacy (CIL) and computational thinking (CT). The authors fit two-level multilevel models (students nested in schools) to estimate intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs), variance explained (R2) at level 1 and level 2, and minimum detectable effect sizes (MDES) under power assumptions (two-tailed test, power=0.80, balanced design P=0.50). They use five plausible values for CIL/CT and average variance components across plausible values, then compute MDES using Hedges and Hedberg’s method. Results show strong country specificity in ICCs (CIL ICC difference 0.44 in 2013 and 0.46 in 2018; CT ICC difference 0.38 in 2018) and that increasing the number of schools (J) substantially lowers MDES, while adding both student and school/teacher covariates (Model 3) yields the most precise effects. Limitations include reliance on design/power quantities rather than causal intervention effects and listwise deletion for missing covariates.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The manuscript does not train or compare machine-learning predictive models; instead, it uses multilevel linear modeling to estimate ICCs, R2, and MDES for CRT power analysis. Therefore, the ML technique fields are intentionally empty (no supervised ML algorithms are evaluated), and the study is classified as exploratory/design-methods rather than predictive ML.
